I didn't like it. The games are essentially just repetitively doing the same things over and over again to get them right once you get the knowledge on how to get them right. Super boring mechanic to be honest. Part 3 was the worst, though, because, what you had originally believed to be the only way to progress the game winds up being the wrong thing to do and the only way to fix it? You guessed it. Start the whole game over from the very end to nearly the very beginning just to get things right because now you know it's bad to do that. The game really genuinely feels like it's just stalling for time until the refund period is over. Also, the mechanics are pretty dull. Aside from strategy (which fundamentally boils down to doing things over and over again until you learn a strategy), there isn't much for the player to do but read (you might as well just pick up a book instead). Fighting is a joke of a mechanic: just decide how hard you're going to hit or use a spell instead--both of which wind up being influenced by the 'do it over until you get it right' approach.

Aside from that, in case you're wondering, the game wasn't buggy for me, and the story is an interesting one, though I wouldn't argue that the writing is stellar.

I also thought I'd add that I've played games before that punish you for not knowing how everything in the game works, and I've enjoyed them. Oxygen Not Included and Don't Starve both will just let you die from a lack of knowledge and make you start over. BUT, you never have to do the exact same events over and over again just to try to get the best outcome. Every replay is fresh because you're doing everything and your choices, while multitudinous, aren't set in stone. You can do anything, no set story line to adhere to, just general survival goals. Honestly? They allow you to truly choose your own story. The Sorcery games just make you read one that's already been written in the most tedious fashion possible. 

I've also played visual novels before and enjoyed them because they didn't have super boring mechanics to ruin their stories.

Sorcery! part 3, is my favorite part by far (out of the four parts). It gives you a more open world type of experience, with a lot to explore. This game features my favorite method of time travel out of any other game. The present is a post apocalyptic wasteland, with the Archmage's seven deadly serpents hunting and stalking you. The past, however, is a green and lush landscape, serpentless, and  with towns to explore. There are towers in the map that allow you to reverse time in the area that you make its light shine on. So, essentially, you can time travel, but only in places where you shine the light (which can only be adjusted from the towers themselves). In real time, you can simultaneously see the landscape become alive in the tower's light and die when outside of the light, which I think looks pretty neat. The dynamic is that travelling in the past is usually safer, however, only a certain amount of the area can be reverted to the past at one time, so the harsh present day cannot be entirely avoided. The seven serpents also help make this part my favorite one because they add to the whole situation, making it much more dire. Each of the seven serpents has an element under their command, they are tough opponents, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, and will either stalk you or lay in wait to trap you. I recommend buying all four parts and playing parts 1 and 2 before part 3, since your character transfers from part to part. Parts 1 and 2 are also sold together, giving a big bang for your buck.

But THIS is the real reaseon you should try this series. The previous two serve as a prelude to the glory of Kakhabad.

So.
It's an open-world. Adventure game. With RPG mechanics. Good writing. Spirit of exploration. Spirit of exploration multiplied by two because there are two timelines that you're exploring: the present where all you see around you is a desloate wasteland devastated by magical cataclysm and the lush past where there's grass and life. After going through the pretty linear first part and a non-linear but grindy second, [i]Seven Serpents[/i] were simply a revelation. There are so many things that can happen to you on your hunt for the seven great lizards! And even when you find them (or they find you) - where's the real guarantee that you won't become their breakfast immediately? So before actually going toe-to-toe with them, you'd better find out what their weaknesses are. Then trick them into a position that would be favorable for you (unless - again - they do the same to you first).

The feeling when I just had an arduous climb to the top of a mountain range, then I rest having a look around, seeing dusk falling on the dried wilderness, and then I notice the first serpent somewhere far in the north - circling a mountain peak... There's little like it.

If in doubt about the [i]Sorcery![/i] franchise - you might as well just try this part and see if you like it. You'll miss out on quite a few things that persist from the previous games, but you'll have all the fun [i]Seven Serpents[/i] has to offer nonetheless.
And if you like it, maybe give others a try - there's a reason [i]Rock Paper Shotgun[/i] gave the complete [i]Sorcery![/i] the title of RPG of the year in 2016.

Quite simply if you liked Steve Jackson & Ian Livingstone FF books then this is a MUST BUY. Inkle has produced far and away the best game saga going. The entire Sorcery! series is an amazing production of Steve Jackson's epic series and this third part is absolutely awesome.

Each game is progressively bigger and better, so that they are so much more than simply an on-screen copy of the gamebook. (Some fighting fantasy games are available from other developers, but are basically just the original book with the highly limited options that a 400 page book allowed.)
There is a massive amount of new material & also rearranging of original material from the books, however all the new material has an authentic feel, in keeping with the source material.

The combat system is a little strange at first, but way better than random dice rolls once it is mastered.

The great thing about these games is the ability to retrace your steps and return to areas already explored (apart from in part 1) and what you find will be influenced by your previous actions. This gives massively more scope than the original books ever could.

The brilliant "double-layered" map in part 3 adds an amazing depth to the game, as each location can be encountered in the [b]present[/b] or the [b]past[/b], providing massively more scope to the plot.

The orchestral theme music, prepared by Laurence Chapman, is simply perfect for this epic quest.

These games are so massive that after over 100 playing hours there are still so many more options in the game to explore that it remains interesting. Thank-you Inkle!
Multiple layers of time travel and enormous non-linearity make this not only the best Sorcery! game, but one of the best RPGs of recent years.

Riprendo il commento usando sempre il libro originale della serie di librogame Sorcery! - Sortilegio (apparsi per EL) come confronto.

Rispetto al primo episodio, molto conservativo, questo nelle Bakland, sulle tracce (inteso sia come preda che come predatore) dei sette serpenti, scombina tutto. Gli sviluppatori hanno dato libera stura alla creatività e hanno creato il loro proprio mondo nel mondo, ispirandosi probabilmente anche a Titan, l'ambientazione creata da Steve Jackson e Ian Livingston per i loro librogiochi. Quindi cos'è che cambia? Che in pratica avremo due interi mondi paralleli che rappresentano epoche diverse fra cui ci muoveremo sfruttando i "fari", misteriose, antiche torri che svettano sul paesaggio. Questa meccanica aggiunge letteralmente una nuova dimensione all'originale, ed è un espediente difficilmente pensabile per un librogame. Di ogni evento e luogo avremo due versioni, spesso interconnesse. Ho l'impressione che le nuove parti scritte appositamente per il videogioco si integrino meglio nella storia che nell'episodio precedente di Kharé. Ho trovato particolarmente suggestivo e ben strutturato l'incontro con la stregona sulla montagna, che introduce un promettente nuovo uso della magia (un'altra novità?).

Quello che comunque sconvolge di più la trama originale è la totale libertà di movimento: si può andare avanti e indietro e ripercorrere ogni luogo senza limiti, e il gioco se ne ricorderà. Quindi, ed è questa la conseguenza fondamentale, è possibile andare meticolosamente a caccia di tutti i serpenti per eliminarli. Viene però allo stesso tempo a mancare quel senso di urgenza e di dover avanzare a tutti costi, anche sulla strada sbagliata, dei Sette Serpenti cartacei, che contribuiva in gran parte all'atmosfera tesa del libro. Viceversa, il famigerato attraversamento del lago Ilklala riuscirà un po' più facile (e non è per nulla necessario passare da Fenestra).

Si può stare sicuri che tutto quello che c'è nel libro (incluse le illustrazioni) si ritrova (magari leggermente modificato) anche qua, in mezzo a tutto il resto, talvolta scombinato sul piano spaziale o temporale.

Andando più nel tecnico: ho trovato non banali i combattimenti, e in media un po' troppo difficili. La magia dovrebbe aiutare di più: penso al libro, dove la pensata giusta al momento giusto risolve quasi tutto. Invece qua un nemico, anche se ferito, mantiene la stessa forza, e spesso si è obbligati a scontrarcisi (vedi serpente lunare). È anche difficile gestire l'abilità, perchè mi sembra troppo facile perderla (sono arrivato ad avere una barra di potenza ridicolmente corta) e non è mai chiaro quando, come e in che misura ciò succede. Sarebbe utile un valore chiaro di Abilità accanto alla Resistenza.

Insomma, il gioco è stato un azzardo riuscito di innovazione di un grande classico e il risultato è encomiabile. Non ha il fascino e la suspence dell'originale, ma è avvincente, non ne tradisce lo spirito e ha molto da offrire anche a chi conosce i librogiochi a menadito! Da appassionato, mi sento di straconsigliarlo!

Sorcery! Part 3 is the third game in the same series developed and published by inkle Studios, the same people behind the 80 Days game. Sorcery! is a faithful adaptation of Steve Jackson's Fighting Fantasy gamebooks of the same name and much like them it features an astoundingly well realized world

The size of world you get to explore is on first glance rather unimpressive but its actually so chock-full of locations you can potentially visit that there is almost no chance you'll be able to see them all even after a couple of playthroughs, there is just so many of them

The writing in Sorcery! is rather excellent. I don't know if it was lifted compltely from the gamebooks or written by the developers themselves but each character has a unique "voice and tone" despite never speaking a single word and the locations are so well described I couldn't help but to get myself immersed in all of it

Besides simply talking your way through problems you can always ignore them and walk away or perhaps use your sword arm or even magic to solve them. However, while the combat presentation is stellar the actual mechanics themselves leave a lot to desire for

Sorcery! Part 3 contains an incredibly well fleshed out world full of realistic characters, interesting locations and plenty of difficult choices to make which come with actual consequences. The combat system might be lackluster but the writing is absolutely top notch and the few issues Sorcery! has can be easily dismissed once you're immersed in to the world

I love this game and all the parts!

A really satisfying continuation of the first two parts, a pleasingly different structure to the game and narrative whilst still sitting solidly within the established world and mechanics. What this installment significantly brings to the table is more-or-less complete freedom of movement, not just around the world map but now being able to switch between two alternate versions of it. I really enjoyed this greater freedom as the first two did boil down to rather linear journeys (still with extremely twisty branching pathways!) This gave much more the feel of a classic text adventure game with survival elements, which I appreciated.

What really stands about these games is the sheer amount of content on offer, I feel like I could play through this a dozen times and still be discovering new secrets and encounters. Steve Jackson has a truly incredible imagination, and the writing is both excellent and extremely clever. The plot threads and the clues to solve the larger puzzles are masterfully interwoven into the fabric of the world, and almost every location you visit yields a new surprise.

Definitely looking forward to seeing what happens in the fourth installment!
